title: Beginning smaller
statement: Dependence is a starting condition, not a verdict on worth.
explanation: Adler saw the child's helplessness among more capable people as a common beginning of inferiority feelings. These feelings can prompt learning and striving; they do not automatically constitute a disorder.
nuance:
A child cannot yet reach, read or decide what adults can. The experience of not yet being able helps organize a movement toward greater competence. Adler asks what direction that movement takes, especially whether it develops with an interest in others.

His theory should not be read as saying that everyone has one secret defect explaining their whole life. A feeling of being less capable is different from actually being less valuable. The response to the feeling, and the social setting around it, are central.
metaphor: A small figure meets a series of uneven steps; the higher position is shown as a possibility of learning.

composition.description: A small figure meets a series of uneven steps; the higher position is shown as a possibility of learning.

title: An answer to difficulty
statement: A limitation does not dictate the single life that follows it.
explanation: Adler's account of compensation concerns efforts to respond to experienced insufficiency. A difficulty can encourage new skills or become the center of a defensive struggle for status.
nuance:
Someone struggling with one activity may practice intensely or find another way of contributing. Adler's early interest in bodily limitations developed into a wider account of psychological and social responses.

Compensation is not the claim that every hardship is secretly a gift. Difficulties can remain painful and opportunities are unequal. What interests Adler is how the person interprets the difficulty and organizes a response, rather than treating one bodily or social condition as an unchangeable destiny.
metaphor: One obstacle branches into different possible routes rather than a single predetermined outcome.

composition.description: One obstacle branches into different possible routes rather than a single predetermined outcome.

title: When less becomes a life
statement: The problem grows when felt inadequacy rules the whole field of action.
explanation: For Adler, an intensified and unresolved sense of inferiority can discourage participation. Instead of treating a difficulty as something to meet, the person organizes life around avoiding exposure to it.
nuance:
A person who assumes any mistake will prove they are worthless may stop attempting tasks they could learn. The complex is not simply modesty or awareness of a skill gap. It concerns the organizing force of the judgment.

Adler asks about the person's goal and relation to others as well as the feeling itself. Removing one obstacle may not help if a demand for complete security still makes every uncertain activity unacceptable. The distinction is between not yet succeeding and treating possible failure as a verdict on existence.
metaphor: A figure retreats from an available test while the imagined measuring line keeps rising.

composition.description: A figure retreats from an available test while the imagined measuring line keeps rising.

title: Toward more
statement: The question is what becoming more capable is for.
explanation: Adler described a movement from felt insufficiency toward greater security, completion or superiority. Its direction matters: developing a capacity with others differs from needing to stand above them.
nuance:
Two people may pursue the same skill. One wants to do useful work; the other wants proof that no one can rival them. Outward achievement alone does not show which aim organizes the effort.

Striving for superiority in Adler's terminology is not always simple domination. His writing distinguishes growth and adaptation from a personal goal of power over others. Reading the phrase only as competitive ambition misses the contrast at the center of his account.
metaphor: A route toward an imagined destination is set beside a shared crossing, asking whether the goal connects or separates.

composition.description: A route toward an imagined destination is set beside a shared crossing, asking whether the goal connects or separates.

title: The elevated position
statement: Looking superior can be a way to avoid feeling inferior.
explanation: Adler interpreted some displays of dominance or importance as answers to threatened self-worth. Being above others promises security while keeping attention fixed on personal rank.
nuance:
Someone who must win every discussion may be protecting a fragile sense of competence rather than expressing stable confidence. That is an interpretive possibility, not a diagnosis that follows from assertiveness alone.

The display can also make cooperation more difficult, preserving the insecurity it tries to escape. Adler's concern is the whole pattern: the imagined danger, the compensating goal and the social effect. Humiliation by others does not become justified because a person has adopted an unhelpful defense.
metaphor: A figure rises on a short pedestal while the neighboring figures remain disconnected from it.

composition.description: A figure rises on a short pedestal while the neighboring figures remain disconnected from it.

title: Room for an imperfect attempt
statement: Participation asks for courage before it offers certainty.
explanation: Adler associated discouragement with withdrawal from life's demands. In his account, courage allows a person to meet a task without first securing an invulnerable image of themselves.
nuance:
A learner who can make a visible error has more room to learn than one who must never appear inexperienced. Courage here is not dramatic fearlessness. It is willingness to take part despite an uncertain result.

The social setting matters: ridicule and impossible demands can make participation harder. Adler's educational emphasis therefore includes how people encourage one another. Telling someone to be brave is a thin substitute for a relationship in which an imperfect attempt is allowed.
metaphor: An uneven bridge develops between two figures instead of requiring one figure to leap the empty gap alone.

composition.description: An uneven bridge develops between two figures instead of requiring one figure to leap the empty gap alone.

title: One direction, many expressions
statement: A person's thoughts, feelings and actions may belong to one way of meeting life.
explanation: Individual Psychology does not mean studying a person in social isolation. Adler's emphasis is the person's unity: apparently separate traits can express an organizing direction within a shared human world.
nuance:
A person may be assertive at home and timid at work. Adler asks whether both stances serve a similar aim, such as avoiding a position of felt weakness. Opposite appearances need not imply wholly separate personalities.

Unity is an interpretive hypothesis about the relation among patterns, not proof that every action follows one conscious plan. Circumstances still matter. The approach looks for a form of orientation while resisting the idea that a trait can be understood apart from the life in which it operates.
metaphor: Thought, feeling and action appear around one figure, then connect with the same uneven route.

composition.description: Thought, feeling and action appear around one figure, then connect with the same uneven route.

title: Ask where it leads
statement: An action can be understood through its aim as well as its origin.
explanation: Adler emphasized purposive movement in mental life. Understanding behavior involves asking what position or outcome it tends toward, not only what earlier event preceded it.
nuance:
A person may avoid a gathering because they fear rejection. Adler also asks what the avoidance secures: perhaps freedom from being tested or a preserved image of independence. The aim need not be a calculated conscious decision.

This approach does not erase history or claim that every painful condition is deliberately chosen. A pattern can acquire a purpose within a life without explaining everything that produced it. The question concerns direction and function, rather than blaming someone for the circumstances they face.
metaphor: A winding route forms toward a faint destination that was present before the movement became clear.

composition.description: A winding route forms toward a faint destination that was present before the movement became clear.

title: The imagined audience
statement: A life organized around being seen can lose contact with the task itself.
explanation: Adler examined vanity as a preoccupation with personal significance and superiority. The person attends to how they appear, while cooperation and the actual demands of a situation become secondary.
nuance:
In a conversation, someone may be composing an impressive answer rather than hearing the problem. The visible action resembles participation, but the organizing interest is the self's rank in an imagined audience.

Wanting recognition is not inherently vanity. Adler's distinction concerns what dominates the relationship: contributing to something shared or securing a special position. The interpretation needs a pattern over time, since one proud moment or desire for appreciation tells little about a whole orientation.
metaphor: A figure is lifted above neighbors while the shared ground remains disconnected.

composition.description: A figure is lifted above neighbors while the shared ground remains disconnected.

title: An indirect position
statement: Compliance can sometimes be a way of organizing the relation.
explanation: Adler treated submissiveness as a pattern whose meaning depends on its direction. Yielding may express cooperation, fear of exposure or an indirect attempt to secure approval and influence.
nuance:
Someone who never disagrees may later feel entitled to have every unstated need understood. Apparent selflessness can coexist with a powerful expectation about what others owe in return. That is one possible pattern, not the meaning of all accommodation.

Real inequalities can make open disagreement unsafe. Adler's interpretation should not turn constrained compliance into a character flaw. The question is how a stance operates in a particular relation, including the power and options available to the person.
metaphor: One figure tilts toward another; the connecting thread remains taut rather than disappearing.

composition.description: One figure tilts toward another; the connecting thread remains taut rather than disappearing.

title: The protected distance
statement: A retreat can preserve safety while making the world smaller.
explanation: Adler interpreted some anxious patterns through their role in avoiding demands and threatened defeat. The fear is real, but the withdrawal can also become part of an organized response to felt inadequacy.
nuance:
Avoiding every evaluative task may reduce immediate distress while preventing experiences that could alter a person's expectation of failure. Adler asks how that arrangement fits the person's wider goal.

Anxiety has many causes and cannot be reduced to a strategic excuse. His functional interpretation concerns some patterns, not every anxious state. It is most useful when it adds a question about the effects of withdrawal without denying distress or the reality of danger.
metaphor: A figure steps back from a possible encounter; a curved detour closes around the familiar safe space.

composition.description: A figure steps back from a possible encounter; a curved detour closes around the familiar safe space.

title: What the feeling does
statement: An emotion changes the distance between people.
explanation: Adler examined anger among affects that can separate people. Besides the felt experience, he attended to its effect on the relation: it can intimidate, distance others or organize a demand for control.
nuance:
An outburst may end a difficult conversation by making everyone else withdraw. That effect does not mean the anger was consciously manufactured. A feeling can be sincere and still become woven into a recurring relational pattern.

Anger can also answer injustice or protect a boundary. Adler's account asks about its direction and social use; it should not make calmness the sole measure of reasonableness. Who is angry, what happened and what follows are all part of the interpretation.
metaphor: A jagged line appears between two figures and their separation increases.

composition.description: A jagged line appears between two figures and their separation increases.

title: A place among others
statement: A family position is experienced, not merely counted.
explanation: Adler studied the family constellation as a relational setting for development. A child's position depends on perceived roles, expectations and comparisons, not simply the number printed beside their birth.
nuance:
Two firstborn children can occupy very different situations if one receives steady attention and the other becomes responsible for younger siblings early. The same ordinal place does not imply the same psychological meaning.

Adler proposed recognizable patterns, but they should not be converted into fixed personality types. His question concerns how a child interprets their place among particular people. Family changes, culture and material circumstances alter the setting within which that place is understood.
metaphor: A child stands among two older figures with uneven connecting lines showing relation rather than a numbered slot.

composition.description: A child stands among two older figures with uneven connecting lines showing relation rather than a numbered slot.

title: Help that takes the task away
statement: Care can become limiting when it prevents a child from practicing participation.
explanation: Adler warned against forms of pampering that teach a child to expect others to arrange life around them. His concern is not affection itself, but care that repeatedly removes opportunities to act and cooperate.
nuance:
An adult who does every manageable task for a child may communicate that the child cannot meet difficulty without rescue. The immediate comfort can carry a longer lesson about dependence and entitlement.

The distinction is between responsive help and replacing all effort. Children need protection and support; withholding care is not a route to courage. Adler's educational aim involves gradually widening participation, with tasks proportionate to the child's capacities rather than demands for premature independence.
metaphor: A protective cage is drawn around a child; its bars cross the space where action might begin.

scene.caption: help that takes the task away

composition.description: A protective cage is drawn around a child; its bars cross the space where action might begin.

title: The unwelcoming world
statement: A child can learn to expect exclusion before they know how to name it.
explanation: Adler connected neglect with a discouraged or hostile orientation toward others. A child who repeatedly experiences the world as unhelpful may have difficulty expecting cooperation or feeling a place within it.
nuance:
If asking for help reliably produces contempt, avoiding dependence can become understandable. Adler investigates how this expectation enters later relationships, including situations that differ from the original one.

This is not a claim that neglect determines one inevitable personality. Supportive relations and changed circumstances matter. Nor does the child's response excuse neglect. The social setting belongs inside the explanation: an isolated account of the child's supposed deficiency would miss the relation that helped shape the expectation.
metaphor: Lines from surrounding figures stop short of the child, leaving the central space without a crossing.

composition.description: Lines from surrounding figures stop short of the child, leaving the central space without a crossing.

title: When the center moves
statement: A new arrival can change the meaning of an older child's place.
explanation: Adler discussed how a firstborn child may experience a sibling's arrival as a loss of a once-exclusive position. What matters is the child's interpretation and the family's response, rather than firstborn status alone.
nuance:
A child formerly receiving most attention may discover that the household now attends to someone else. They may respond through responsibility, rivalry, cooperation or withdrawal. Adler's account offers possible directions, not an automatic prediction.

The familiar label of a dethroned firstborn compresses a complicated transition. A welcoming preparation, available care and the child's existing relations can change its meaning. The picture should prompt a question about a changed position rather than assign a permanent role.
metaphor: Attention that first rests above one child slowly shifts toward a second figure.

composition.description: Attention that first rests above one child slowly shifts toward a second figure.

title: The view from behind
statement: Being surrounded by more capable siblings can invite effort or discouragement.
explanation: Adler described different possible responses to the youngest child's position. Feeling behind may encourage energetic attempts to catch up, or produce a retreat from comparison when the others seem unreachable.
nuance:
A younger child might develop an activity no sibling has claimed, becoming capable through a different route. Another may decide that competition is hopeless and rely on special treatment. Adler presents these as contrasting possibilities.

The useful distinction is the meaning assigned to the situation, rather than a birth-order stereotype. Age gaps, disability, family change and how siblings treat each other all modify the experience. The youngest position is a setting in which development occurs, not a sealed description of the person.
metaphor: A lower figure faces a branching route: one path follows the steps, while another leads to a different task.

composition.description: A lower figure faces a branching route: one path follows the steps, while another leads to a different task.

title: The child's account
statement: The same household can contain different experienced worlds.
explanation: Adler emphasized the child's interpretation of circumstances. A family event can acquire different significance for different children, shaping distinct expectations about belonging, ability and recognition.
nuance:
One sibling can experience a parent's demanding attention as encouragement while another hears a verdict of inadequacy. Neither interpretation follows automatically from the family's outward arrangement.

This focus on meaning should not obscure actual harm or unequal treatment. A child's interpretation is not the only thing happening. Adler's approach is strongest when it considers both the social situation and the child's response to it, rather than choosing between an entirely objective environment and an entirely private story.
metaphor: One shared event sends two uneven lines toward different destinations.

composition.description: One shared event sends two uneven lines toward different destinations.

title: The selected world
statement: An outlook helps determine which details become important.
explanation: Adler treated perception as active selection within a person's orientation to life. Two people can meet the same situation while attending to very different evidence of danger, possibility or rank.
nuance:
At a gathering, one person notices openings for conversation while another notices only signs of rejection. Adler asks how the selection fits a larger expectation and goal. The surroundings are real, but they are not attended to neutrally.

This does not mean every discouraging observation is invented. Sometimes exclusion is present. The point is to distinguish what happens from the pattern of significance through which it is encountered. A repeated selection can narrow the experienced world without making that world wholly imaginary.
metaphor: A figure directs a gaze toward one marked detail while other details remain faint at the edge.

composition.description: A figure directs a gaze toward one marked detail while other details remain faint at the edge.

title: The chosen beginning
statement: An early memory can show a present orientation as well as a past event.
explanation: Adler was interested in which early memories a person retains and emphasizes. He treated recollections as clues to a pattern of outlook, rather than complete objective records of childhood.
nuance:
A person might remember being alone while others played, using that scene as an image of their place in the world. Adler asks what the selection and telling express now, as well as what may have happened then.

A recollection's emotional force does not independently verify all its details. Memory is selective, and a useful interpretation need not turn the scene into the single cause of the person's life. The memory provides a point of inquiry into meaning, not an infallible origin story.
metaphor: A present figure looks toward a framed earlier scene; a line isolates one remembered part of it.

composition.description: A present figure looks toward a framed earlier scene; a line isolates one remembered part of it.

title: Rehearsing a position
statement: Fantasy can prepare a response before the situation arrives.
explanation: Adler related imagination and fantasy to the person's direction of striving. Imagined scenes can rehearse possible action, anticipated defeat or a gratifying position that ordinary life does not yet provide.
nuance:
Someone may repeatedly imagine being admired while avoiding the uncertain work that could develop a skill. Another uses imagination to try out a cooperative response before a difficult meeting. The activity looks similar; its direction differs.

Adler's interest lies in what the imagined scene does within a life. Fantasy is not automatically evasion, and preparation is not automatically accurate. A scenario can widen possible action or repeatedly confirm the expectation that action is unsafe.
metaphor: A small stage appears around a figure, presenting a possible role before any real encounter takes place.

composition.description: A small stage appears around a figure, presenting a possible role before any real encounter takes place.

title: A feeling for the next move
statement: Adler asked how a dream prepares an attitude toward a problem.
explanation: Unlike Freud's emphasis on disguised wish-fulfilment, Adler interpreted dreams through the person's orientation and current difficulties. A dream can produce a mood that supports a particular way of meeting what comes next.
nuance:
A frightening dream before a demanding encounter might make retreat feel more justified. Adler would explore how the mood fits the person's larger pattern, rather than decode the dream through one universal set of symbols.

This is an Adlerian interpretation, not a demonstrated account of every dream. The person may not consciously intend the result. The important contrast with Freud concerns the question asked: what direction does the dream support, rather than only what earlier wish it transforms?
metaphor: An imagined stage sends a line toward a future route, showing how a scene can orient the next movement.

scene.caption: a feeling for the next move

composition.description: An imagined stage sends a line toward a future route, showing how a scene can orient the next movement.

title: What becomes difficult to notice
statement: An apparent failure of attention can be connected with a person's aim.
explanation: Adler investigated attention, distraction and some forms of forgetting through their relation to tasks and social demands. He asked whether the selection serves a wider pattern of avoiding exposure or responsibility.
nuance:
A person remembers details connected with recognition but repeatedly overlooks a shared obligation. Adler would look for the direction of that pattern instead of treating each lapse as entirely separate.

This is not a reason to assume that all forgetfulness is deliberate or interpret difficulties of attention as poor character. Ordinary distraction, health and circumstance have their own relevance. The hypothesis concerns how selective attention may participate in a life pattern, and it needs more than one convenient anecdote.
metaphor: Several details surround a figure, but only the one aligned with the familiar route receives a connecting line.

composition.description: Several details surround a figure, but only the one aligned with the familiar route receives a connecting line.

title: A small world to practice in
statement: Play lets a child try relations before they have to hold them for real.
explanation: Adler saw play as preparation for life, revealing interests and ways of relating. A child can experiment with roles, cooperation, power and competence in situations that do not carry every adult consequence.
nuance:
Building together, playing teacher or inventing a contest offers different positions toward others. Adler would observe how the child participates, including whether a role makes room for companions or chiefly secures superiority.

One game is not a personality test. Children explore, imitate and change their rules. The value of observing play lies in its living relations and possibilities for encouragement, rather than assigning a permanent trait to each toy or role.
metaphor: A child approaches an unfinished small construction, with several places where action could begin.

scene.caption: a small world to practice in

composition.description: A child approaches an unfinished small construction, with several places where action could begin.

title: Belonging with others
statement: The person is never a self-made island.
explanation: Adler's social feeling concerns participation in a shared human world. It includes the capacity to cooperate and take others into account, rather than merely feeling sociable or wanting approval.
nuance:
A quiet person doing reliable shared work may express more social interest than a charming person who treats companions as an audience. The criterion is the relation to a common life, not how outgoing the personality appears.

Adler treats social embeddedness as fundamental: language, care and survival depend on others. His account is therefore ethical as well as psychological. It asks how striving connects with shared life, without making constant friendliness or agreement the measure of a person's value.
metaphor: Two figures build opposite halves of a bridge until a shared crossing exists between them.

composition.description: Two figures build opposite halves of a bridge until a shared crossing exists between them.

title: A task between us
statement: Working together changes the question from rank to contribution.
explanation: Adler contrasted concern with personal superiority against participation in communal tasks. A shared problem offers a different orientation: what needs doing, and how can each person take part?
nuance:
Two people carrying something awkward need to adjust to each other. If one insists on proving they are stronger, the task may become harder for both. Cooperation concerns responsiveness to the relation, not merely performing equal movements.

A shared aim does not remove differences of skill, interest or power. Nor does it require yielding to unfair demands. Adler's emphasis asks whether the arrangement supports common life, rather than using community as a word that excuses one person's dominance.
metaphor: Two figures connect to opposite sides of one uneven load; the load rises only as their relation develops.

composition.description: Two figures connect to opposite sides of one uneven load; the load rises only as their relation develops.

title: Another point of view
statement: Understanding someone asks for movement beyond your own position.
explanation: Adler discussed empathy and identification as ways of approaching another person's experience. Seeing from their place requires more than attributing one's own preferences to them.
nuance:
What seems an easy choice from outside may involve obligations or fears visible only from the other person's situation. Trying to occupy that perspective can alter the explanation of their conduct.

Empathy does not guarantee accuracy, and imagined identification can become projection. The other person can correct the account. Adler's social emphasis makes understanding an encounter with another position, rather than possession of a hidden psychological key that removes the need to listen.
metaphor: A curved route runs from one figure around the shared space toward the place occupied by the other.

composition.description: A curved route runs from one figure around the shared space toward the place occupied by the other.

title: The shared ground
statement: Private certainty still has to meet a world inhabited by others.
explanation: Adler connects individual conduct with the requirements of communal life. A person's private justification can feel complete while failing to account for the needs and experiences of those around them.
nuance:
Someone might defend never asking for help as perfect independence, while relying invisibly on other people's labor. Adler asks how a personal account relates to the actual conditions that make life possible.

Community is not automatically wise or just. Collective demands can also exclude and dominate. The useful question concerns reciprocity and reality: who contributes, who carries the cost, and whose experience the supposedly self-sufficient explanation leaves outside its frame?
metaphor: One figure is placed between supporting figures and uneven connecting lines, making the invisible relations visible.

composition.description: One figure is placed between supporting figures and uneven connecting lines, making the invisible relations visible.

title: The social ladder
statement: A judgment of inferiority can be built into the culture around a child.
explanation: Adler criticized the cultural privileging of men and the assumption that women were inherently inferior. He connected some struggles over identity and worth with unequal social valuation rather than natural deficiency.
nuance:
A girl repeatedly told that competence belongs to boys may confront both a practical barrier and an interpretation of her place. Adler's account locates that pressure within a social hierarchy, not simply inside her confidence.

His own writing also carries assumptions of its period, so this critique should not be presented as a complete contemporary theory of gender. Its relevant move is to examine how a society manufactures comparative value, and how people organize responses to that arrangement.
metaphor: Two similar figures stand on unequal platforms; the supporting social structure is drawn between them.

composition.description: Two similar figures stand on unequal platforms; the supporting social structure is drawn between them.

title: A place to attempt
statement: Encouragement widens participation rather than awarding a superior rank.
explanation: Adler's educational approach emphasizes conditions in which children can develop courage and social feeling. Respectful help supports an attempt without making the child's worth depend on defeating someone else.
nuance:
Compare being told that only the best child deserves attention with being helped to contribute to a shared task. The second setting gives an imperfect effort a place in the relation. It can encourage competence without requiring superiority.

Encouragement is not indiscriminate praise or denial of difficulty. An attempt can need correction while still being welcomed. Adler's concern is how feedback affects the child's direction: toward engagement with others, or toward protecting a fragile position in a hierarchy.
metaphor: Two figures form a shared bridge with room for an incomplete section, allowing progress without a perfect first attempt.

composition.description: Two figures form a shared bridge with room for an incomplete section, allowing progress without a perfect first attempt.
